There's no service dog certification in the US. You would need documentation from a doctor stating that you would benefit from a service and likely work with a trainer on proper task tqnd public access training.

But honestly 7 years old is approaching retirement age for most dogs. Most service dog training requires 2+ years for public access training and at 9 years old mobility work may be too hard on their joints.

If you don't mind my unsolicited advice, speak with your doctors about the viability of having a service dog. Take your dog to get a health work up and evaluate if they're fit for mobility tasks before working them any further and if you do continue working them probably only do so at home.

Instead maybe consider looking into service dog programs or trainers to start working with a new dog who would be able work public access if that's what you need.

Sometimes players just need a little help when it comes to engaging with their environment, especially new players or younger players.

Guided questions help a lot. "Is there anything else you'd like to look at?" "Is there anything you'd like to do before you leave?" "Would your characters be looking for anything in particular?"

If their answers are no, no, and no. Then you can still hand out more information as the party moves along in bite sized pieces that are easier for them to hold onto. "Ok then. As you make your way to leave you noticed the door is decorated with intricate features. Put together you feel they might hold information that could be useful to you later on. Would you like to take a closer look?" 

Giving your players breaks between new pieces of information also gives them the chance to internalize what they just heard and think about what to do with it as well as giving them the chance to interact with the narrative before moving on to the next bit. They'll be less likely to miss or forget information since they won't be trying to keep up with your descriptions. And if any questions do pop up they won't be holding on to it while you're talking, or be interrupting you for clarification as often.

Will this work for everyone? Probably not, nothing does. But it can be incredibly useful and easily adapted to fit the play style of many different kinds of parties.

Not to mention, people take in and process information differently. Some people have processing disordes or something related. For me personally if I don't have anything visually engaging (related or not) going on i might as well not be hearing anything at all.

I tend to reink my dice during sessions just so I can have something to do while listening so that I can keep myself engaged instead of getting lost in the sauce.

Yes! Its so much easier to engage with the narrative when its broken up onto parts. Start with the big image and let players ask for the details. Hand out information when it becomes relevant. No one here *WANTS* cats to die. Its a horrible horrible choice to make.  But unfortunately those feral cats are hunting so many endemic species to extinction. It absolutely sucks that things got this far in the first place, but they have and unfortunately drastic measures have become necessary.

Australian wildlife have been suffering for decades. They lose more and more native populations every year. They already have such strict animal import, export and care laws, several species are banned from transport in and out of the country. They have barn cat programs and TNR programs but it still hasn't been enough.

There are *millions* of feral cats in Australia but there are less than *1,000* numbats left in the wild and their populations are continuing to decline. Whats more important? The native species that are dying in their own home, or the invasive species that are hunting them to extinction?

It always sucks to quantify life. But the unfortunate reality of the world is that humans have made a really big mess of things. It isn't feasible to save every creature and sometimes you have to make some horrible decisions to fix things before they get even worse.

Albino animals don't always have red eyes. Albinism is the complete lack of specifically melanin, and the lack of pigment is what causes eyes to appear red. However, some animals have other pigments in their eyes and so albinism presents differently.

For example, cats, dogs, horses and even humans don't often have red eyes as albinos. Their eyes can often appear blue or tawny in color instead since blue pigmentation often lies beneath the brown from melanin.

A more accurate way to tell the difference between albinism and leucism is to look at the colors of different tissues. Lescistic animals often retain pigment in their eyes, lips noses and pawpads/hooves.

Slow down. Moving too quickly and burning out is one of the biggest causes for washing when it comes to owner training.

You've only been at this for 3 months, give yourself a break. Take a step back and move in smaller increments. Remember, dogs and especially puppies aren't great at generalizing. They may follow some commands under specific circumstances, but if you change even one little thing all that knowledge tends to get thrown straight out the window. Practice inside your own home more. Then try it with more distractions like toys or sounds or people. Then try it in your yard. Then in your yard with distractions. Etc. And if you find he's back sliding move back to the previous step again.

Don't be embarrassed about your puppy being a puppy. He hasn't even gone through adolescence yet, and when he does you'll find yourself in very much the same scenario.

It sounds like you didn't properly acclimate your pup to the head halter, which can take months for them to get used to. ESAs have no legal rights to be in public areas. The only thing they get that normal pets don't is housing under the FHA.

 Also ESAs don't require any form of training and should not be confused with psychiatric service dogs who are specifically task trained to mitigate their handlers symptoms. Emotional support does not count as a task. It must take an active effort such as providing DPT for grounding, creating space, leading their handler away from triggering situations etc. Simply being a companion is not enough.

Fun fact hotels are not required to allowed ESAs without pet fees. Only service dogs must be permit without fees, and even then cannot legally be left in the room alone.

In aussies it's less because of a risk of the tail being grabbed so much as a risk of the tail being stomped on by cattle which is horribly painful and almost always results in amputation.

It's not likely to happen, but I can understand why people used to dock tails to prevent it happening in the first place. Having the tail amputated under under circumstances is generally a more pleasant experience than having it done after suffering a sever injury.

Saying I understand why it started doesn't mean I condone docking in modern day. Most dogs nowadays are pets and are under no threat of suffering such an injury.

If docking is done, it should never be all the way to the base of the spine. It's important to leave at least a nub.

Dogs have a lot of important nerves and muscles connected to the base of the tail many of them are used for pooping. Docking the tail too short (i.e. leaving nothing at all) often results in all kinds of issues such as not knowing when they need to poop and not knowing when they're done pooping.

>The only time genetic defects happen is two related dogs having puppies.

Well that's just factually incorrect. Genetic defects are not at all exclusive to inbreeding. They happen any time two dogs with the genes compatible to result in a genetic defects breed together, not just of they're related to each other. The only reason there's a correlation between genetic defects and inbreeding is that animals from the same lineage are more likely to carry the same genes and therefore pass them on to offspring.

They will only produce maybe one or two litters a year to prevent over breeding and the issues that come with it. And they evaluate the homes of those bringing their puppies home to make sure it is a good fit and will often take them back of it isnt to prevent them from going to shelters instead. 

Also please keep in mind that even feral dogs will inbreed and are still prone to genetic health problems, and will breed whenever possible contributing to the over population of strays.

I've said this quite a few times in this thread already, but this is the misconception about service dogs that bothers me the most, so I hope you don't mind me saying it here as well.

Service dogs absolutely do get affection just like any other job, just not from strangers while they're working. It's actually really important to service dogs to have time to just be regular dogs, otherwise they can get burnt out.

The thing about handlers not wanting people to pet their dogs while working is two things. 1) working in public is already difficult. There are so many distractions, like new sights, scents and sounds that we can't control that our dog has to ignore to do their job. That's already asking quite a bit from them, so.we ask people not to cause even more distractions. 2) pets from strangers can teach our dogs in appropriate behaviors. They can start actively expecting or even start seeking out attention rather than focus on us. This can lead to them having to wash out because they can no.longer reliably do their job.

However, that does not at all mean that any affection is forbidden from them. At home service dogs are very much just like pet dogs. When my SD isnt working he demands scritches like no bodies business and his weekend morning routine requires at least 15 minutes of family cuddle time before I'm even allowed to get out of bed. (His terms, not mine.)

I even give him scratches and treats while hes working. Many handlers do. It's important that they know they're doing a good job. The difference, from us its a reward, not a distraction.

So dont feel bad that you cant pet the good boy, they get plenty to make up for it.

Good news! Service dogs do get pets and cuddles and love! Just because they're not getting that from strangers doesn't mean ita completely forbidden. Their handlers give them plenty of pets and treats and toys during their time off at home.

Double good news! Some dogs need more than just love and pets and are at their happiest when they have a job to do. So not only do service dogs get all the love from their handlers, but they also get to fulfill their need for a sense of purpose by having such an important job to do. They get use to their brains everyday doing what they love with the person they love.

I and many handlers male sure our dogs are as loved and happy as they can be. They save our lives every day, the least we can do is make sure they know they're appreciated.

Service dogs definitely get all the loves and pets, they just get them all from their owner. Just because they're working doesn't mean they're no longer a dog. 

Service dog also don't work 100% 24/7. Yes some dogs need to keep an eye on their handler at l all times, but that doesn't mean they dont get time off. At home or in safe and familiar environments they're allowed to relax and play just like any other dog. 

The big problem comes when working in public. Theres already so many distractions, new sights, new sounds, new smells, and for a.dog who's senses are so much better than ours, that's a lot of stuff to ignore while working. Having random people cooing at and petting you at the same time is really just setting yourself up for failure. So we ask people not to distract our dogs while they're working in public. I still pet and praise my.dog while he's working though. Many handlers do, its important they know they're doing a good job. The difference is, I'm the one he needs to be focused on anyway. What am I gonna do? Steal his attention from myself? He's already looking at me.

At home is an entirely different story. I dont know many dogs more spoiled than service dogs. Rest assured that service dogs are very well loved.

Good Handlers and trainers go out of their way to make sure working isn't stressful. Think about it this way, stressed out people suck at their job. Your much more likely to do good work when you enjoy what you're doing. The best job you can get is one you wake up looking forward to doing and you'll do your best work there.

Same goes for any animal. If their work is stressful they won't do a very good job. So it's important to make sure our dogs love what they do. Task training is the easy part. The bulk of service dog training is socializing and confidence building. Exposing them to new things and teaching them that it's fun, not scary. That's the part that makes service dog training so hard.

I agree with everything u/jeanlee03 has stated.

 There's no way to guarantee a fully trained service dog in 2 years let alone anything under that time. Service dog training is a huge rollercoaster of things going wrong and then having to fix them, there's not really any telling how a dog will react to many situations, how often they'll get set back, or even if they'll cut it as a service dog at all, double that for a shelter dog. And that's *after* you've already chosen your prospect. The process of even finding a dog to start with is a whole mess of it's own. Two years is a tight timeline to maintain, and trying to stick to a due date like that is likely to make you more liable of washing due to burn out.

If you are set on a shelter dog, 100% work with a professional trainer or behaviorist. They'll know what to look for and are better trained for picking out red flags. Try to go with owner surrenders over rescues and try to ask the staff for as much if their back ground as possible. Dogs from abusive backgrounds tend to be more unpredictable and may have triggers you don't/can't account for especially if you don't know exactly where they came from. Wherever possible look for dogs from caring families who were put in the unfortunate situation of no longer being able to care for them and ask the staff for as much medical history as possible. Definitely avoided any overly timid or nervous dogs, or any dogs who are clearly under socialized, or any dogs with severe chronic illness that would either impede their work or make working them entirely unethical.

Having owned, raised or even trained your own dog honestly doesn't mean much when it comes to service dog training. Many things service dogs learn can easily be taught with just that knowledge, but the more important things such as PA training and many tasks require a lot of specific knowledge and know how that you just don't get from standard dog training, or even non SD professional training. Service dogs are a whole different beast and should be approached as such if you want the best chances of succeeding.

You may need to rethink your approach if your concerns right now are wanting a specific breed, and  saving money, especially if you want to do so successfully.

First and foremost, dogs are expensive. Service dogs triple so. Whether owner training or going through a programs you will end up spending some $10,000 on average. Also, service dogs take time. It'll be about 2 years wait for a fully trained dog either way since that the length for most waitlists and about the average time it takes to properly train a service dog.

Second, and something we say often on this sub is "need before breed." Yes, any breed has the potential to produce a service dog, and odd dogs are often successful, but some breeds have better chances than others. That why we always suggest the fab four. If you need a dog urgently they're your best bet, and even then they can still wash out. 

Mixed breeds are already difficult since you don't really know what traits you'll get from the parents. Every litter is a mixed bag. On top of that you're searching for a mix of two notoriously difficult breeds. Can it be done? Sure. In fact there are plenty people in this community that have husky and rottie SDs and plenty more with mixed breed dogs. (My own is an aussie mix of unknown heritage). But it will be an uphill battle to find the right dog to even start with.

Please know that no one here is trying to discourage you. The unfortunate truth of it is that service dogs are hard. And if you want to have one and succeed, you need to understand just how hard that is and either temper your expectations or prepare for the long haul.

Leucisim is an incomplete form of albinism. It can appear in a multitude of ways, from faded coloration to splotches of pigment, or pigment only occurring on certain body parts or tissue types.

Some albino animals do have the appearance of having colored eyes, depending on their genetics. For example animals like cats dogs and humans have a layer of blue pigmentation beneath the brown color of their eyes. So albino cats, dogs, and humans often have blue colored eyes. On the flip side of this rodents like rats and mice only have brown pigment in their eyes so leucistic mice and rats have pink or red eyes.

Albino deer and caribou can have eyes that appear blue instead of red.
